analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance to cover surgery for children's birth defects and disfiguring injuries.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted 97 cosponsors from both parties, but it was referred to three committees and two subcommittees and never received a vote in any of them or on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required group health plans, employer plans, and individual insurance policies that cover surgery to also cover diagnosis and treatment of a child's congenital deformity, developmental disorder, or injury — up to age 21 or 22, depending on the type of plan. It was aimed at cases where insurers deny operations to correct conditions like cleft lip and palate as "cosmetic," leaving families to pay out of pocket. It would have covered any treatment the child's physician deemed medically necessary to approximate a normal appearance, including procedures that do not improve physical function and follow-up care, while still allowing insurers to use pre-authorization and excluding purely cosmetic surgery on normal bodies.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 22 born with or having developed disfiguring or function-impairing conditions — cleft lip and palate, craniofacial differences, deformities from burns, trauma, infection, or tumors — and their families. Under the bill, a family whose plan covers surgery could no longer be refused payment because a needed operation was labeled cosmetic; the insurer would have to cover treatment the treating physician called medically necessary to approximate a normal appearance, including secondary procedures and follow-up care. Families who today pay thousands of dollars out of pocket, or forgo recommended surgeries, would have had them covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children with birth defects and their families

how_it_helps.text: Any group health plan or health insurer that covers surgical benefits would have to cover outpatient and inpatient diagnosis and treatment of a child's congenital or developmental deformity, disease, or injury.

Coverage would include any surgical treatment the treating physician deems medically necessary to approximate a normal appearance — including procedures that do not improve physical function and follow-up treatment for secondary conditions — which closes the common insurer loophole of calling corrective surgery 'cosmetic' and denying it.

The requirement reached nearly all coverage pathways: it amended the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code, and applied to both group plans and individual insurance, with an effective date of January 1, 2010.
The bill still allowed plans to apply pre-authorization and pre-certification rules, and explicitly excluded cosmetic surgery on normal structures of the body, limiting the mandate's scope.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers and employers would bear the added cost of the required benefit, likely passed along as somewhat higher premiums for all enrollees and higher benefit costs for self-insured employers. Insurers would keep pre-authorization authority, but would lose the ability to deny medically necessary reconstructive surgery on children as cosmetic.

drawbacks.text: The mandate would raise insurance premiums for all plans covering surgical benefits, since the cost of procedures insurers might otherwise deny — including reconstructive surgery that does not improve physical function — would be spread across all enrollees rather than borne only by affected families.

The 'medically necessary to approximate a normal appearance' standard is subjective and would invite disputes between families and insurers, and the bill preserved pre-authorization and pre-certification requirements, so plans could still delay or deny claims and force families to appeal.

The mandate applied to self-insured employer plans through ERISA, so employers would bear higher benefit costs directly, which in a tight economy could show up as reduced wages or benefits elsewhere rather than only in premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and specific: children with disfiguring congenital conditions would no longer depend on their parents' ability to pay, and the bill tried to guard against abuse by carving out purely cosmetic surgery and preserving insurers' pre-authorization rights. The cost is higher premiums spread across everyone with coverage and added administrative burden on employers and insurers, and the "approximate a normal appearance" standard is subjective enough that it would have generated coverage disputes rather than eliminating them. On balance, a well-targeted mandate whose modest costs were outweighed by the harm it prevented, but it was a narrow fix that would have been partly overtaken by broader coverage legislation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to three House committees, then to subcommittees, and no committee ever voted to send it to the floor, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Carolyn McCarthy of New York introduced the bill on March 5, 2009, with an initial list of co-sponsors that included Republicans such as Pat Tiberi, Roscoe Bartlett, John McHugh, and Frank Wolf.
It ultimately drew 97 cosponsors — 75 of the House's 253 Democrats and 22 of its 178 Republicans — giving it clear bipartisan support.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees on the day it was introduced; within a month it was further referred to subcommittees on health.

No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the action history shows nothing after the April 29, 2009 subcommittee referral — so the bill never came to a vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were better off because the coverage mandate never became law and they avoided paying for childhood reconstructive surgery they could otherwise deny as cosmetic. Families of children with conditions like cleft lip and palate continued to fight insurers or pay out of pocket for operations their plans refused to cover.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and employers avoided the mandate

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 97 cosponsors split 75 Democrats and 22 Republicans, and the bill died in committee without any vote, so no party bloc ever had to oppose it on the record.

industries.note: The bill forced insurers covering surgical benefits to pay for reconstructive surgery for children's birth defects, developmental conditions, and injuries — including procedures that improve appearance but not function, which plans commonly deny as cosmetic. Insurers would lose the ability to shift those costs to families, and would gain new premium revenue only to the extent prices rose.
Because the bill amended ERISA, large employers that fund their own health plans would have had to add this benefit to their employees' coverage, raising their benefit costs.

industries.industry: Reconstructive and plastic surgeons, hospitals, and surgical facilities
industries.note: Mandated coverage would make more childhood reconstructive procedures insurable, increasing the volume of surgeries that families can actually afford and reducing uncompensated and charity care for cleft and craniofacial repair.
